name: claude-memory-kit
description: Persistent memory with hooks, wiki, and daily synthesis for multi-project workflows
readme:
![Claude Memory Kit](.github/assets/og-banner-claude-code.png) # Claude Memory Kit **Built-in memory decides what to remember. This one asks.** Claude Memory Kit is a Claude Code plugin that gives your coding agent a memory made of plain text files in your own folder. Session two opens with *"you were on Nestlé, the client hates em-dashes, next step: the Q3 brief"* — without you explaining anything again. The agent notes small facts as dated lines and tells you; nothing becomes a rule or a knowledge article until you say yes. No database, no service, no API key. An independent project, not made or endorsed by Anthropic. **Optional second half, for people who delegate to subagents:** a method that ships with it — specs written as files before work starts, a subagent's report treated as a claim until checked, review findings that turn into checks. [![Version](https://img.shields.io/github/v/release/awrshift/agent-memory-kit?label=version&color=CFEF4A&cacheSeconds=1800)](https://github.com/awrshift/agent-memory-kit/releases) [![License: MIT](https://img.shields.io/badge/License-MIT-55503E?labelColor=55503E&color=55503E)](LICENSE) [![Claude Code plugin](https://img.shields.io/badge/Claude_Code-plugin-CFEF4A)](#install) **On this page:** [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#install) · [What is inside the plugin](#what-is-inside-the-plugin) · [What it creates in your folder](#what-it-creates-in-your-folder) · [The method](#the-method-for-work-with-subagents) · [Why not built-in memory](#why-not-the-built-in-memory) · [Privacy and cost](#privacy-and-cost) ## How it works ![How Claude Memory Kit works: you talk, the agent writes plain files in your folder, hooks load them at the next start](.github/assets/01-system-map-claude-code.png) 1. **You talk.** "We're working on Nestlé." "The client hates em-dashes." You never open a memory file. 2. **The agent writes.** Something worth keeping becomes one dated line in `MEMORY.md`, and the agent tells you ("saved", with the line). The work itself (backlog, specs, research, decisions) goes into that client's own folder, `projects//`. 3. **You close the day.** Say "we're done for today". The agent looks for patterns across dates ("you rejected em-dashes on four different days, make it a rule?"), writes what you approve, and leaves a handoff note. 4. **Tomorrow starts already knowing.** At the next session start a hook loads the memory, the newest handoff and the knowledge index. Nothing becomes a rule without your yes, and every line carries its date, so a stale fact looks stale. ## Install Inside the folder you work in, in Claude Code: ```shell /plugin marketplace add awrshift/agent-memory-kit /plugin install memory-kit@memory-kit /memory-kit:setup ``` `setup` reads what the folder already has and **proposes before writing anything**; your `CLAUDE.md` stays yours. Git is optional. To upgrade later: `claude plugin marketplace update memory-kit`, then `claude plugin update memory-kit@memory-kit` (the full id is needed), and restart the session. Upgrades never touch your files. ## What is inside the plugin A plugin install hides its file tree, so here is all of it. ![What is inside the plugin: seven hooks, ten skills, four agents](.github/assets/06-whats-inside.png) ### Hooks — run by themselves | Hook | When | What it does | |---|---|---| | `session-start.py` | every session start, and after a compaction | Loads the working agreement, your `MEMORY.md`, the newest handoff and the knowledge index. Warns when memory is over its caps, when a path in memory no longer exists, when a spec is waiting for your ratification, and when your project wires its own copy of a kit hook (it would run twice). | | `pre-compact.sh` | before the conversation is compacted | A manual `/compact` waits until memory is saved and inside its caps. An automatic compaction is never blocked (that would fail your request); if it ran over unsaved memory, the next context opens with "save memory now". | | `protect-tests.py` | before a file edit | Asks before an edit that could weaken an existing test: an assertion changed or removed, a `.skip` or `.only` added. New tests pass silently. | | `guard-git.py` | before a shell command | Stops force push, `push --mirror`, `reset --hard`, `clean -f`, `branch -D`, `checkout .`. `--force-with-lease` passes. | | `guard-secrets.py` | before a read, edit or shell command | Keeps `.env` files, keys and certificates out of the transcript, whether by a file tool, a shell command or a redirection. One exception: a single literal `echo` or `printf` appending a line to `.env`. | | `guard-zsh-split.py` | before a shell command, in zsh only | Catches a variable that zsh will NOT split into words the way bash does, before the command silently does the wrong thing. | | `session-end.sh` | when the session ends | Writes one timestamp line, nothing else. | The guards for git and secrets block the action if they crash or time out, instead of letting it through (Claude Code 2.1.295 or later; older versions accept the setting but let the action through). Each guard names its opt-out variable. In a folder that never ran `setup`, the hooks write nothing. Shared code in `hooks/lib/`: `cmdparse.py` (one shell-command parser for every guard), `rails.py` (permission settings facts), `stale-refs.py` (finds paths in memory that no longer exist), `legacy_hooks.py` (spots a project's own copy of a kit hook), `statefs.py` and `state.sh` (write the kit's state files safely: never through a symlink, never outside the project). ### Skills — you call them, or just say what you want All are named `/memory-kit:`, and each one also triggers from plain words. Until a skill runs, only its one-line description sits in the context. | Skill | What it does | |---|---| | `close-session` | The end-of-day ritual: capture what is new, look for patterns on 3+ dates, promote on your yes, refresh the memory header, write the handoff. | | `memory-audit` | When memory trips a cap: a table of moves (to the knowledge base, to a rule, or out) for your approval, then the moves. | | `system-audit` | The periodic health check of the whole setup through seven lenses; it measures which layers actually fired and proves each guard through its real wiring. | | `setup` | Adopts the kit in this folder, settles how it coexists with Claude Code's own auto memory, and offers safe permission rails. | | `tour` | A walkthrough of the kit on your own files. | | `session-review` | An adversarial review of a session's work by an isolated reviewer that reads the actual files. | | `second-opinion` | Independent reviewers on one high-stakes decision before it reaches you. If you already run your own review board, use that instead. | | `qa-sweep` | A multi-lens QA pass over your running product, every finding with repro steps. | | `document` | A PR description, changelog entry, release note or postmortem, written only from the actual `git diff`. | | `code-sync` | After a merge, reconciles each spec's status with what the code now shows. | ### Agents — workers your agent delegates to | Agent | Model | What it does | |---|---|---| | `executor` | Opus | Builds to a decided spec in its own git worktree. Never redesigns; any deviation is reported. Stops if a value it must produce has no source in the spec. | | `recon` | Sonnet | Read-only fact gatherer: raw facts with file and line, official sources for anything outside the repo. Never designs. | | `idea-validator` | Opus | An isolated critic with none of your conversation, so it cannot anchor on your framing. | | `qa` | Sonnet | One QA lens on the running product (user flow, edge states, honesty, contract, UX). Observes, never fixes. | ### Rule templates — the always-loaded part you opt into A plugin cannot install rules, so `setup` offers these and copies them only on your yes. | Template | What it holds | |---|---| | `templates/rules/orchestration.md` | Nine invariants for working with subagents ([listed below](#the-method-for-work-with-subagents)). | | `templates/rule-template.md` | The shape of a good rule: one checkable always/never, scoped by `paths:` so it loads only where it applies. | ### Reference — depth, read only when needed | Doc | Read it when | |---|---| | `reference/spec-depth.md` | Writing a spec: the depth pass, checking outside facts fresh, review by stake, failure branches written first, measuring the outcome rather than a proxy. | | `reference/orchestrator-fact-check.md` | Accepting anyone's report: how a claim becomes a fact, and the cheapest decisive check per kind of claim. | | `reference/review-loop.md` | Handling findings: triage to the layer that owns them, the review gate on diffs, the registry that turns a repeated mistake into a check. | | `reference/parallel-development.md` | Fanning work out: worktrees, one integrator, when to go sequential. | | `reference/doc-governance.md` | Keeping docs true: one home per fact, dated status, nothing cited from a temp folder. | | `reference/decisions-log.md` | Recording a product or architecture decision in a lean ledger. | | `reference/project-extensions.md` | Adding your own rule, skill, hook or agent, and what each costs while idle. | | `reference/harness-measurement.md` | Changing settings or hooks: prove it with a fixed probe set before and after. | | `reference/capability-map-sweep.md` | Code duplicates what an installed library already does. | | `reference/qa-PROTOCOL-TEMPLATE.md`, `reference/qa-mcp.json.example` | Setting up `qa-sweep` for a product. | ### Templates, scripts and the agreement - **Memory files:** `templates/MEMORY-TEMPLATE.md`, `templates/HANDOFF-TEMPLATE.md`, `templates/workspace/knowledge-index.md`. - **Per project:** `templates/workspace/project/README-TEMPLATE.md` (the project's map and workflow tier), `BACKLOG-TEMPLATE.md`, `SPEC-TEMPLATE.md` (the contract an executor builds to), `ASSUMED-SPEC-TEMPLATE.md` (an executor's recorded override, owed your ratification). - **Other:** `EXPERIMENT-TEMPLATE.md` and `experiments-README.md` (a sandbox for throwaway work), `ONBOARDING-BACKLOG.md` (a first day in five tasks), and the four `document` templates (`pr.md`, `changelog.md`, `release-note.md`, `postmortem.md`). - **Scripts:** `scripts/quiet.sh` (runs a noisy command, keeps the full log in a file, prints a summary), `scripts/permission-probes.sh` (checks that your permission rules stop what they should); `system-audit` carries `collect.sh`, `gates.py` and `usage.py`. - **The working agreement:** `context/identity.md`, injected at every session start. It is the kit's only always-on instruction text, about 1.6k tokens. ``` plugins/memory-kit/ ├── hooks/ hooks.json · session-start.py · pre-compact.sh · protect-tests.py · guard-git.py │ guard-secrets.py · guard-zsh-split.py · session-end.sh · lib/ · tests/ ├── skills/ close-session · memory-audit · system-audit · setup · tour · session-review │ second-opinion · qa-sweep · document · code-sync ├── agents/ executor · recon · idea-validator · qa ├── reference/ the depth docs above ├── templates/ memory · rules · workspace · project ├── scripts/ quiet.sh · permission-probes.sh └── context/ identity.md ``` ## What it creates in your folder Only state, and only after `setup`: ``` your-folder/ ├── .claude/memory/MEMORY.md hot cache: dated one-liners, capped at 180 lines / 32 KB / 3000 chars a line ├── context/handoffs/ one note per session; the newest is loaded at the next start ├── knowledge/ the wiki: one article per settled topic, written after your yes ├── .claude/rules/ always / never, only what you promoted └── projects// each client's own documents: README (the map), BACKLOG, plans/, research/ ``` ```mermaid flowchart LR T([you talk]) --> H["MEMORY.md
dated one-liners"] H -->|"/close-session"| N["handoffs/
one note per session"] H -->|"same pattern on 3+ dates
and you say yes"| K["knowledge/
facts + rationale"] K -->|"stable, mechanical"| R["rules/
always / never"] N -->|"newest one loaded"| S([next session]) H -->|"loaded in full"| S ``` A pattern's path: a dated line, then (seen on 3+ dates, with your yes) a knowledge article, then (stable and mechanical) a rule. **Memory vs paperwork:** what the agent learned is shared across your work; what the work produced belongs to one client's folder. Say "now IKEA" and the agent reads that folder only. ## The method for work with subagents ![Agent-orchestrated work: the main session writes a spec file, four agents work from it, and a report is input, never a fact](.github/assets/07-orchestrated-work-v73.png) The main session designs and decides; subagents build or gather facts from a spec written as a file before anyone starts. The nine invariants in `templates/rules/orchestration.md`, in plain words: 1. A report from a subagent or reviewer is input, not a fact. Re-run the check, read the line, look at one real output yourself. 2. Subagents build to a decided spec file and never redesign; a deviation is reported, not absorbed. 3. A value with no named source stops the build as an owed decision; nothing is invented. 4. The main session alone writes memory and project documents, merges, and re-runs every check on the merged result. 5. A failing test means the code is wrong, not the test. 6. Reviewers are judged on merits, never by counting votes. 7. A subagent is resumed only for a short follow-up; new work gets a fresh one with a brief that points at files. 8. Every number in a report comes from a script or command shown next to it. 9. Scope, anything others will see, irreversible data changes and spending are yours to decide; technical choices are the agent's, explained as "decision, why it is correct, what would prove it wrong". A spec also carries three lines before it is handed over (`reference/spec-depth.md`): a **depth pass** (what a top expert in the field would do that nobody asked for), a **practice** line (outside facts checked against official sources today, with the date), and a **review** line (who reviews it, by stake). Failure branches are written before the run, and success is judged by what reaches the user, not by a counter. ## Why not the built-in memory? Claude Code ships its own auto memory, on by default. It is effortless, and it lives outside your folder. | | Claude Code auto memory | Claude Memory Kit | |---|---|---| | Who decides what is remembered | the agent, silently | the agent proposes, **you approve** | | Where it lives | `~/.claude/projects/`, on this machine only | **plain files in your folder** | | Can you read it, diff it, fix a wrong belief | partly | **yes, it is text** | | One memory per client | no | **yes**, `projects//` | | Shared with a teammate or a second machine | no | **yes**, it is in the repo | | How staleness shows | it doesn't | **every line is dated**; caps force a prune | | Cost at session start | up to 200 lines / 25 KB (Claude Code docs) | about 6.5–8.5k tokens on three working repositories (measured 2026-09-26), bounded by the caps, plus ~2k of skill and agent descriptions | Running both means two writers and two truths, so `setup` asks you to pick one. ## Privacy and cost - **The kit itself sends nothing.** No hook or script opens a network connection; all are readable Python or shell. Claude Code sends what it reads, memory included, to the model, as with any file in the conversation. - **Private by default.** The hot cache and handoffs are gitignored, so they stay local even if you push. The knowledge base and rules are tracked: keep the repository private or prune before publishing. Working from two machines or with a teammate? Say so at `setup` and the hot cache gets committed instead. - **Forgot to close the session?** Nothing breaks: the next session still opens with your memory. You lose that session's handoff note and the pattern audit. ## Origin Built and used daily by one operator since March 2026, across marketing, research and product work, and the method behind several production agent setups. Layers that quietly rotted were retired (a daily journal, a rolling status file, a staging layer), and CI now checks on every push that the memory actually reaches the model and that this page lists every part of the plugin. A 68-second recording of a real session: [demo video](.github/assets/demo-full-session.mp4). **Tell me how your first week went:** [open a note](https://github.com/awrshift/agent-memory-kit/issues/new?template=first-week.md). [Architecture](docs/ARCHITECTURE.md) · [Claude Code facts](docs/specs/claude-code.md) · [Changelog](docs/CHANGELOG.md) · [Contributing](docs/CONTRIBUTING.md) · [Open decisions](docs/DECISIONS.md) · MIT, see [LICENSE](LICENSE).

Claude Memory Kit

Built-in memory decides what to remember. This one asks.

Claude Memory Kit is a Claude Code plugin that gives your coding agent a memory made of plain text files in your own

folder. Session two opens with *"you were on Nestlé, the client hates em-dashes, next step: the Q3 brief"* — without

you explaining anything again. The agent notes small facts as dated lines and tells you; nothing becomes a rule or a

knowledge article until you say yes. No database, no service, no API key.

An independent project, not made or endorsed by Anthropic.

Optional second half, for people who delegate to subagents: a method that ships with it — specs written as files

before work starts, a subagent's report treated as a claim until checked, review findings that turn into checks.

![Version](https://github.com/awrshift/agent-memory-kit/releases)

![License: MIT](LICENSE)

![Claude Code plugin](#install)

On this page: [How it works](#how-it-works) · [Install](#install) · [What is inside the plugin](#what-is-inside-the-plugin) ·

[What it creates in your folder](#what-it-creates-in-your-folder) · [The method](#the-method-for-work-with-subagents) ·

[Why not built-in memory](#why-not-the-built-in-memory) · [Privacy and cost](#privacy-and-cost)

How it works

![How Claude Memory Kit works: you talk, the agent writes plain files in your folder, hooks load them at the next start](.github/assets/01-system-map-claude-code.png)

1. You talk. "We're working on Nestlé." "The client hates em-dashes." You never open a memory file.

2. The agent writes. Something worth keeping becomes one dated line in MEMORY.md, and the agent tells you

("saved", with the line).

The work itself (backlog, specs, research, decisions) goes into that client's own folder, projects/<client>/.

3. You close the day. Say "we're done for today". The agent looks for patterns across dates ("you rejected

em-dashes on four different days, make it a rule?"), writes what you approve, and leaves a handoff note.

4. Tomorrow starts already knowing. At the next session start a hook loads the memory, the newest handoff and the

knowledge index. Nothing becomes a rule without your yes, and every line carries its date, so a stale fact looks stale.

Install

Inside the folder you work in, in Claude Code:


/plugin marketplace add awrshift/agent-memory-kit

/plugin install memory-kit@memory-kit

/memory-kit:setup

setup reads what the folder already has and proposes before writing anything; your CLAUDE.md stays yours.

Git is optional. To upgrade later: claude plugin marketplace update memory-kit, then

claude plugin update memory-kit@memory-kit (the full id is needed), and restart the session. Upgrades never touch

your files.

What is inside the plugin

A plugin install hides its file tree, so here is all of it.

![What is inside the plugin: seven hooks, ten skills, four agents](.github/assets/06-whats-inside.png)

Hooks — run by themselves

| Hook | When | What it does |

|---|---|---|

| session-start.py | every session start, and after a compaction | Loads the working agreement, your MEMORY.md, the newest handoff and the knowledge index. Warns when memory is over its caps, when a path in memory no longer exists, when a spec is waiting for your ratification, and when your project wires its own copy of a kit hook (it would run twice). |

| pre-compact.sh | before the conversation is compacted | A manual /compact waits until memory is saved and inside its caps. An automatic compaction is never blocked (that would fail your request); if it ran over unsaved memory, the next context opens with "save memory now". |

| protect-tests.py | before a file edit | Asks before an edit that could weaken an existing test: an assertion changed or removed, a .skip or .only added. New tests pass silently. |

| guard-git.py | before a shell command | Stops force push, push --mirror, reset --hard, clean -f, branch -D, checkout .. --force-with-lease passes. |

| guard-secrets.py | before a read, edit or shell command | Keeps .env files, keys and certificates out of the transcript, whether by a file tool, a shell command or a redirection. One exception: a single literal echo or printf appending a line to .env. |

| guard-zsh-split.py | before a shell command, in zsh only | Catches a variable that zsh will NOT split into words the way bash does, before the command silently does the wrong thing. |

| session-end.sh | when the session ends | Writes one timestamp line, nothing else. |

The guards for git and secrets block the action if they crash or time out, instead of letting it through (Claude Code

2.1.295 or later; older versions accept the setting but let the action through). Each guard

names its opt-out variable. In a folder that never ran setup, the hooks write nothing.

Shared code in hooks/lib/: cmdparse.py (one shell-command parser for every guard), rails.py (permission settings

facts), stale-refs.py (finds paths in memory that no longer exist), legacy_hooks.py (spots a project's own copy of a

kit hook), statefs.py and state.sh (write the kit's state files safely: never through a symlink, never outside the

project).

Skills — you call them, or just say what you want

All are named /memory-kit:<name>, and each one also triggers from plain words. Until a skill runs, only its one-line

description sits in the context.

| Skill | What it does |

|---|---|

| close-session | The end-of-day ritual: capture what is new, look for patterns on 3+ dates, promote on your yes, refresh the memory header, write the handoff. |

| memory-audit | When memory trips a cap: a table of moves (to the knowledge base, to a rule, or out) for your approval, then the moves. |

| system-audit | The periodic health check of the whole setup through seven lenses; it measures which layers actually fired and proves each guard through its real wiring. |

| setup | Adopts the kit in this folder, settles how it coexists with Claude Code's own auto memory, and offers safe permission rails. |

| tour | A walkthrough of the kit on your own files. |

| session-review | An adversarial review of a session's work by an isolated reviewer that reads the actual files. |

| second-opinion | Independent reviewers on one high-stakes decision before it reaches you. If you already run your own review board, use that instead. |

| qa-sweep | A multi-lens QA pass over your running product, every finding with repro steps. |

| document | A PR description, changelog entry, release note or postmortem, written only from the actual git diff. |

| code-sync | After a merge, reconciles each spec's status with what the code now shows. |

Agents — workers your agent delegates to

| Agent | Model | What it does |

|---|---|---|

| executor | Opus | Builds to a decided spec in its own git worktree. Never redesigns; any deviation is reported. Stops if a value it must produce has no source in the spec. |

| recon | Sonnet | Read-only fact gatherer: raw facts with file and line, official sources for anything outside the repo. Never designs. |

| idea-validator | Opus | An isolated critic with none of your conversation, so it cannot anchor on your framing. |

| qa | Sonnet | One QA lens on the running product (user flow, edge states, honesty, contract, UX). Observes, never fixes. |

Rule templates — the always-loaded part you opt into

A plugin cannot install rules, so setup offers these and copies them only on your yes.

| Template | What it holds |

|---|---|

| templates/rules/orchestration.md | Nine invariants for working with subagents ([listed below](#the-method-for-work-with-subagents)). |

| templates/rule-template.md | The shape of a good rule: one checkable always/never, scoped by paths: so it loads only where it applies. |

Reference — depth, read only when needed

| Doc | Read it when |

|---|---|

| reference/spec-depth.md | Writing a spec: the depth pass, checking outside facts fresh, review by stake, failure branches written first, measuring the outcome rather than a proxy. |

| reference/orchestrator-fact-check.md | Accepting anyone's report: how a claim becomes a fact, and the cheapest decisive check per kind of claim. |

| reference/review-loop.md | Handling findings: triage to the layer that owns them, the review gate on diffs, the registry that turns a repeated mistake into a check. |

| reference/parallel-development.md | Fanning work out: worktrees, one integrator, when to go sequential. |

| reference/doc-governance.md | Keeping docs true: one home per fact, dated status, nothing cited from a temp folder. |

| reference/decisions-log.md | Recording a product or architecture decision in a lean ledger. |

| reference/project-extensions.md | Adding your own rule, skill, hook or agent, and what each costs while idle. |

| reference/harness-measurement.md | Changing settings or hooks: prove it with a fixed probe set before and after. |

| reference/capability-map-sweep.md | Code duplicates what an installed library already does. |

| reference/qa-PROTOCOL-TEMPLATE.md, reference/qa-mcp.json.example | Setting up qa-sweep for a product. |

Templates, scripts and the agreement

  • Memory files: templates/MEMORY-TEMPLATE.md, templates/HANDOFF-TEMPLATE.md, templates/workspace/knowledge-index.md.
  • Per project: templates/workspace/project/README-TEMPLATE.md (the project's map and workflow tier),

BACKLOG-TEMPLATE.md, SPEC-TEMPLATE.md (the contract an executor builds to), ASSUMED-SPEC-TEMPLATE.md (an

executor's recorded override, owed your ratification).

  • Other: EXPERIMENT-TEMPLATE.md and experiments-README.md (a sandbox for throwaway work), ONBOARDING-BACKLOG.md (a first

day in five tasks), and the four document templates (pr.md, changelog.md, release-note.md, postmortem.md).

  • Scripts: scripts/quiet.sh (runs a noisy command, keeps the full log in a file, prints a summary),

scripts/permission-probes.sh (checks that your permission rules stop what they should); system-audit carries

collect.sh, gates.py and usage.py.

  • The working agreement: context/identity.md, injected at every session start. It is the kit's only always-on

instruction text, about 1.6k tokens.

├── hooks/        hooks.json · session-start.py · pre-compact.sh · protect-tests.py · guard-git.py

│                 guard-secrets.py · guard-zsh-split.py · session-end.sh · lib/ · tests/

6. Reviewers are judged on merits, never by counting votes.

7. A subagent is resumed only for a short follow-up; new work gets a fresh one with a brief that points at files.

8. Every number in a report comes from a script or command shown next to it.

9. Scope, anything others will see, irreversible data changes and spending are yours to decide; technical choices are

the agent's, explained as "decision, why it is correct, what would prove it wrong".

A spec also carries three lines before it is handed over (reference/spec-depth.md): a depth pass (what a top

expert in the field would do that nobody asked for), a practice line (outside facts checked against official

sources today, with the date), and a review line (who reviews it, by stake). Failure branches are written before

the run, and success is judged by what reaches the user, not by a counter.

Why not the built-in memory?

Claude Code ships its own auto memory, on by default. It is effortless, and it lives outside your folder.

| | Claude Code auto memory | Claude Memory Kit |

|---|---|---|

| Who decides what is remembered | the agent, silently | the agent proposes, you approve |

| Where it lives | ~/.claude/projects/, on this machine only | plain files in your folder |

| Can you read it, diff it, fix a wrong belief | partly | yes, it is text |

| One memory per client | no | yes, projects/<client>/ |

| Shared with a teammate or a second machine | no | yes, it is in the repo |

| How staleness shows | it doesn't | every line is dated; caps force a prune |

| Cost at session start | up to 200 lines / 25 KB (Claude Code docs) | about 6.5–8.5k tokens on three working repositories (measured 2026-09-26), bounded by the caps, plus ~2k of skill and agent descriptions |

Running both means two writers and two truths, so setup asks you to pick one.

Privacy and cost

  • The kit itself sends nothing. No hook or script opens a network connection; all are readable Python or shell.

Claude Code sends what it reads, memory included, to the model, as with any file in the conversation.

  • Private by default. The hot cache and handoffs are gitignored, so they stay local even if you push. The

knowledge base and rules are tracked: keep the repository private or prune before publishing. Working from two

machines or with a teammate? Say so at setup and the hot cache gets committed instead.

  • Forgot to close the session? Nothing breaks: the next session still opens with your memory. You lose that

session's handoff note and the pattern audit.

Origin

Built and used daily by one operator since March 2026, across marketing, research and product work, and the method

behind several production agent setups. Layers that quietly rotted were retired (a daily journal, a rolling status

file, a staging layer), and CI now checks on every push that the memory actually reaches the model and that this page

lists every part of the plugin.
